'''tradotto''' (trä-dot′tō), ''a.'' [It., pp. of ''tradurre'', transpose: see ''traduce''.] In ''music'', transposed; arranged.

¶
'''tradrille†''', ''n.'' Same as ''tredille''. ''Lamb'', Mrs. Battle on Whist.

¶
'''traduce''' (trạ-dūs′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''traduced'', ppr. ''traducing''. [= F. ''traduire'' = Sp. ''traducir'' = Pg. ''traduzir'' = It. ''tradurre'', transfer, translate, < L. ''traducere'', bring or carry over, lead along, exhibit as a spectacle, display, disgrace, dishonor, transfer, derive, also train, propagate, < ''trans'', across, + ''ducere'', lead: see ''duct''. Cf. ''transduction''.] '''1†.''' To pass along; transmit.

{{smaller block|It is not in the power of parents to ''traduce'' holiness to their children.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', The Angel and Zachary.}}}}

{{smaller block|From these only the race of perfect animals were propagated, and ''traduced'' over the earth.
{{right|''Sir M. Hale.''}}}}

{{smaller block|To this it is offered that the Soul ''traduced'' is from the woman only.
{{right|''Evelyn'', True Religion, I. 167.}}}}

'''2†.''' To transfer; translate; arrange under another form.

{{smaller block|Oftentimes the auctours and writers are dispraised, not of them that can ''traduce'' and compose workes, but of theim that cannot vnderstande theim, and yet lesse reade theim.
{{right|''Golden Boke'', Prol. (''Richardson.'')}}}}

'''3†.''' To hold up; exhibit; expose; represent.
readings.c1s2:
¶
{{smaller block|For means of employment, that which is most ''traduced'' to contempt is that the government of youth is commonly allotted to them. {{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, i.}}}}

{{smaller block|The removing of Liturgie he ''traduces'' to be don onely as a thing plausible to the People.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xvi.}}}}

4. To misrepresent; hold up or expose to ridicule or calumny; defame; calumniate; vilify.

{{smaller block|If I am
''Traduced'' by ignorant tongues, . . . let me say
'Tis but the fate of place, and the rough brake
That virtue must go through.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., i. 2. 72.}}}}

5†. To draw aside from duty; lead astray; seduce.

{{smaller block|I can never forget the weakness of the ''traduced'' soldiers. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')}}}}

=Syn. 4. ''Defame, Calumniate'', etc. See ''asperse.''

'''traducement''' (trạ̄-dūs′ment), ''n.'' [< ''traduce'' + ''-ment.''] The act of traducing; misrepresentation; defamation; calumny; obloquy.

{{smaller block|Rome must know
The value of her own; 'twere a concealment
Worse than a theft, no less than a ''traducement'',
To hide your doings. {{right|''Shak.'', Cor., i. 9. 22.}}}}

'''traducent''' (trạ̄-dū′sent), ''a.'' [< L. ''traducen(t-)s'', ppr. of ''traducere'', traduce: see ''traduce.''] Slandering; slanderous. [Rare.]

'''traducer''' (trạ̄-dū′sėr), ''n.'' One who traduces, in any sense; especially, a slanderer; a calumniator.

{{smaller block|He found both spears and arrows in the mouths of his ''traducers.'' {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Balm of Gilead, v. 2.}}}}

'''traducian''' (trạ̄-dū′shian), ''n.'' [< LL. ''traducianus'', < L. ''tradux'', a branch or layer of a vine trained for propagation, < ''traducere'', lead along, train, propagate: see ''traduce''.] In ''theol.'', a believer in traducianism.

'''traducianism''' (trạ̄-dū′shian-izm), ''n.'' [< ''traducian'' + ''-ism''.] In ''theol.'', the doctrine that both the body and the soul of man are propagated, as opposed to ''creationism'', which regards every soul as a new creation out of nothing. Also called ''generationism''.

{{smaller block|The theory of ''Traducianism'' maintains that both the soul and body of the individual man are propagated. It refers the creative act mentioned in Gen. i. 27 to the human nature, or race, and not to a single individual merely. It considers the work of creating mankind de nihilo as entirely completed upon the sixth day; and that since that sixth day the Creator has, in this world, exerted no strictly creative energy.
{{right|''Shedd'', Hist. Christian Doctrine, II. 13.}}}}

'''traducianist''' (trạ̄-dū′shian-ist), ''n.'' [< ''traducian'' + ''-ist''.] A traducian. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''traducible''' (trạ̄-dū′si-bl), ''a.'' [< ''traduce'' + ''-ible''.] 1†. Capable of being derived, transmitted, or propagated.

{{smaller block|Though oral tradition might be a competent discoverer of the original of a kingdom, yet such a tradition were incompetent without written monuments to derive to us the original laws, because they are of a complex nature, and therefore not orally ''traducible'' to so great a distance of ages.
{{right|''Sir M. Hale.''}}}}

2. Capable of being traduced or maligned. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''trafficker''' (traf′ik-ėr), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''trafficker''; < ''traffic''(''k'') + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who traffics; one who carries on commerce; a merchant; a trader: often used in a derogatory sense.

{{smaller block|Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre, the crowning city, whose merchants are princes, whose ''traffickers'' are the honourable of the earth?
{{right|Isa. xxiii. 8.}}}}

{{smaller block|His Grace of Norfolk, a bon vivant surrounded by men who kept the table in a roar, and a famous ''trafficker'' in boroughs.
{{right|''E. Dowden'', Shelley, I. 133.}}}}

'''trafficless''' (traf′ik-les), ''a.'' [< ''traffic'' + ''-less''.] Destitute of traffic or trade. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''traffic-manager''' (traf′ik-man″āj-ėr), ''n.'' The manager of the traffic on a railway, canal, or the like.

'''traffic-return''' (traf′ik-rē-tėrn″), ''n.'' A periodical statement of the receipts for goods and passengers carried, as on a railway or canal.

''tragacanthe'' = Sp. ''tragacanto'', ''tragacanta'' = Pg. ''tragacanto'' = It. ''tragacanta'', ''dragante'', gum, OIt. also ''tragacante'', the shrub, < L. ''tragacanthum'', also corruptly ''dragantum'', ML. also ''tragagantum'', ''tragantum'', gum tragacanth, < ''tragacantha'', < Gr. τραγάκανθα, τραγάκανθος, a shrub (''Astragalus gummifer'') producing gum tragacanth; lit. ‘goat-thorn,’ < τράγος, a goat, + ἄκανθα, thorn.] A mucilaginous substance, the product of several low, spiny shrubs of the ge-

It exudes through natural fissures and through incisions, forming respectively vermicelli and leaf or flake tragacanth. It is without smell, and nearly tasteless. Its characteristic, though not largest, element is bassorin. In water}}
readings.c3s4: it swells and disintegrates into an adhesive paste, but, except a small portion, does not dissolve. Tragacanth is emollient and demulcent, little given internally, however, on account of its insolubility. Its chief use in pharmacy is to impart firmness to pills, lozenges, etc. It is also made into a mucilage, particularly for marbling books, and is used as a stiffening for crapes, calicoes, etc. Also called ''gum dragon'', ''dracanth'', and (frequently) ''gum tragacanth''.—'''African tragacanth.''' Same as ''Senegal tragacanth''.—'''Compound powder of tragacanth.''' See ''powder''.—'''Hog-tragacanth,''' various mixtures of inferior gums, used occasionally in marbling books.—'''Indian tragacanth.''' Same as ''Kuteera gum'' (see ''gum''<sup>2</sup>), which includes, besides the product of ''Cochlospermum Gossypium'', that of ''Sterculia urens'' and probably other sterculias.—'''Senegal tragacanth,''' a substance nearly identical with the Indian tragacanth, produced abundantly by ''Sterculia Tragacantha''.

An interchange of goods, merchandise, or property of any kind between countries, communities, or individuals; trade; commerce. {{smaller block|It hath in solemn synods been decreed . . .

A piece of business; a transaction. {{smaller block|The fearful passage of their death-mark'd love . . .
Is now the two hours' ''traffic'' of our stage. {{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., Prol.}}}} {{smaller block|I referre you then to the Ambassages, Letters, ''Traffiques'', and prohibition of ''Traffiques'' . . . which happened in the time of king Richard the 2. {{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', To the Reader.}}}} '''6.''' To trade; pass goods and commodities from one person to another for an equivalent in goods or money; buy and sell wares or commodities; carry on commerce. {{smaller block|Despair to gain doth ''traffic'' oft for gaining. {{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 131.}}}} {{smaller block|At twentie yeares they may ''traffike'', buy, sell, and circumuent all they can. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 193.}}}} 2. Its chief use in pharmacy is to impart firmness to pills, lozenges, etc. It is also made into a mucilage, particularly for marbling books, and is used as a stiffening for crapes, calicoes, etc. Also called ''gum dragon'', ''dracanth'', and (frequently) ''gum tragacanth''.—'''African tragacanth.''' Same as ''Senegal tragacanth''.—'''Compound powder of tragacanth.''' See ''powder''.—'''Hog-tragacanth,''' various mixtures of inferior gums, used occasionally in marbling books.—'''Indian tragacanth.''' Same as ''Kuteera gum'' (see ''gum''2), which includes, besides the product of ''Cochlospermum Gossypium'', that of ''Sterculia urens'' and probably other sterculias.—'''Senegal tragacanth,''' a substance nearly identical with the Indian tragacanth, produced abundantly by ''Sterculia Tragacantha''.
